## Why This Is Asked
This tests practical, end-to-end secrets management in a production Kubernetes platform, including CI checks and runtime enforcement.

## Key Concepts
- Secrets Store CSI and SecretProviderClass
- Rotation annotation and 30-day policy
- OPA Gatekeeper / policy-as-code
- CI gate design and runtime validation
- Minimal manifests for both Deployment and SecretProviderClass

## Code Example
```javascript
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-service
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: registry.example/payments:2.3.1
        volumeMounts:
        - name: secret-volume
          mountPath: /mnt/secrets
      volumes:
      - name: secret-volume
        csi:
          driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io
          readOnly: true
          volumeAttributes:
            secretProviderClass: "aws-secrets-provider"
```

```javascript
apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1
kind: SecretProviderClass
metadata:
  name: aws-secrets-provider
spec:
  provider: "aws"
  parameters:
    secrets: |
      - secretName: db-password
```

```javascript
metadata:
  annotations:
    secretRotationDays: "30"
```

- How would you test rotation without affecting users?
- How do you handle rotation failures and rollback?
- What are trade-offs of Secrets Store CSI vs. in-cluster secret managers?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Real-world multi-tenant data platforms require strong admission control to enforce image provenance and host security postures across clouds. Gatekeeper with Rego enables centralized policy with testable manifests.

## Key Concepts
- Open Policy Agent Gatekeeper
- ConstraintTemplate and Constraint objects
- Image provenance: registry, non-latest, digest
- Pod hardening: resources, securityContext, privilegeEscalation
- Namespace labeling and admission scope
- CI validation: conftest, gatekeeper audit, sample manifests

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (ImageProvenanceAndSecurity)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: imageprovenance
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: ImageProvenanceConstraint
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
      rego: |
        package imageprovenance
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          some i
          container := input.review.object.spec.template.spec.containers[i]
          image := container.image
          startswith(image, "registry.example.com/")
          not endswith(image, ":latest")
          some digest := input.review.object.spec.template.spec.containers[i].imageDigest
          msg := "image must be from registry.example.com with digest"
        }
```
```yaml
# Constraint (ImageProvenanceConstraint)
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ImageProvenanceConstraint
metadata:
  name: require-provenance
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
```

```yaml
# Failing manifest: unsigned or latest, missing resources
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: data-processor
  namespace: data
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: proc
        image: registry.example.com/data/processor:latest
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
```

```yaml
# Passing manifest: compliant image, resources, and securityContext
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: data-processor
  namespace: data
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: proc
        image: registry.example.com/data/processor@sha256:abcdef...
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test policy changes locally before applying to cluster?
- How would you roll out a breaking policy change across multiple namespaces without downtime?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests end-to-end security design for multi-cloud Kubernetes workloads, focusing on identity, secret management, and policy enforcement with real-world tools.

## Key Concepts
- Zero-trust workload identity (SPIRE)
- Ephemeral credentials (Vault)
- Service mesh security (Istio, mTLS, AuthorizationPolicies)
- Policy-as-code (OPA/Rego)
- Egress controls to data lake and namespace isolation

## Sample Solution

### 1. SPIRE Workload Identity
```yaml
# spire-workload.yaml
apiVersion: spire.spiffe.io/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterSPIFFEID
metadata:
  name: data-platform-workload
spec:
  names:
    - data-service
    - analytics-service
    - etl-service
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      environment: production
```

### 2. Vault Integration for Secrets
```yaml
# vault-secret-store.yaml
apiVersion: secrets.hashicorp.com/v1beta1
kind: VaultSecret
metadata:
  name: data-lake-credentials
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  vaultAddress: https://vault.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:8200
  path: secret/data-lake
  provider: hcp
  refreshInterval: 1h
```

### 3. Istio AuthorizationPolicy
```yaml
# istio-authz.yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: data-lake-access
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: data-lake-gateway
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["spiffe://data-platform/data-service"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
        paths: ["/v1/tables/*"]
```

### 4. OPA Policy Example
```rego
#.rego
package kubernetes.admission

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  input.request.namespace == "restricted"
  not input.request.object.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  msg = "Pods must run as non-root"
}

allow[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Deployment"
  input.request.object.spec.template.spec.containers[_].securityContext.privileged
  msg = "Privileged containers not allowed"
}
```

### 5. CI Enforcement Check
```yaml
# .github/workflows/security-scan.yml
name: Security Scan
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  opa-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run OPA policy check
        run: |
          opa eval --fail-defined-deny \
            --data policy.rego \
            --input manifests/
```

## Key Takeaways
- SPIRE provides cryptographically secure workload identity
- Vault enables dynamic secret rotation without application changes
- Istio mTLS ensures service-to-service encryption
- OPA/Rego enforces admission control and runtime policies

questions.explanation:
## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates the ability to design admission-time policy enforcement for sensitive data in multi-tenant environments. It tests understanding of tying secret handling to external stores, per-tenant encryption keys, and namespace-level controls—all critical for regulated workloads in cloud-native platforms.

## Key Concepts

- **Policy as Code (OPA/Rego)**: Declarative policies evaluated at admission control time, enabling infrastructure teams to enforce security and compliance requirements programmatically.

- **Secrets Management**: SecretStore/CSI driver integration allows secrets to be sourced from external stores with envelope encryption using tenant-managed KMS keys, ensuring cryptographic isolation between tenants.

- **Multi-Tenancy**: Namespace-level labeling combined with EncryptionPolicy CRDs provides a declarative mechanism to enforce tenant boundaries and encryption requirements across all namespaced resources.

- **Admission Control**: Gatekeeper policies act as validation webhooks that intercept resource creation and modification requests, blocking non-compliant resources before they enter the cluster.

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to enforce cross-cloud data provenance and model lineage for ML workloads; ensures reproducibility and auditing of deployments.

## Key Concepts
- Policy-as-code with Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper
- Image digests, internal registries, provenance annotations
- MLflow tracking integration and run_id propagation
- Local and CI validation strategies

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: enforce-ml-provenance
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Fail
  rules:
  - name: require-provenance-annotations
    match:
      resources:
        kinds:
        - Deployment
    validate:
      message: 'Missing provenance annotations: model_version, dataset_hash, training_run_id'
      pattern:
        metadata:
          annotations:
            model_version: '*'
            dataset_hash: '*'
            training_run_id: '*'
  - name: require-image-digest
    match:
      resources:
        kinds:
        - Deployment
    validate:
      message: 'Container image must include a digest'
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              containers:
              - image: '*@*'
```

```yaml
# Failing Deployment (no provenance)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ml-inference-fail
  annotations:
    model_version: v1
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ml
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: predictor
        image: registry.internal/ml/predictor:latest
```

```yaml
# Passing Deployment (with provenance and digest)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ml-inference-pass
  annotations:
    model_version: v1.2.3
    dataset_hash: sha256:abcdef1234567890
    training_run_id: tr-789
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ml
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: predictor
        image: registry.internal/ml/predictor@sha256:12345abcdef
```

## Local Verification
- kyverno test <policy.yaml> <test.yaml>
- conftest with YAML schemas for Kubernetes objects

## CI Verification
- Run policy gate in CI on pull requests; ensure failing manifests block merges and passing manifests are allowed.

# Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate sketch (simplified)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: gputypematch
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: GPUsTypeConstraint
  targets:

## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates a candidate's ability to design enterprise-grade, policy-driven security controls across hybrid Kubernetes environments. It tests practical knowledge of admission controllers, supply chain security, and multi-cloud consistency—skills essential for platform engineers and security architects.

## Key Concepts

### 1. Image Provenance and Digest Pinning
Digest pinning ensures immutable deployments by locking images to specific content-addressable hashes (e.g., `sha256:abc123...`). This prevents supply chain attacks through tag manipulation. The policy requires images to be referenced by digest rather than mutable tags like `latest` or `v1.2.3`.

### 2. Sigstore Attestations
Sigstore provides cryptographic verification of software supply chain provenance. By validating attestations against allowed signers, organizations ensure that only images built and signed by trusted parties can be deployed. This integrates with the Sigstore transparency log for auditability.

### 3. SBOM Validation
Software Bill of Materials (SBOMs) provide a complete inventory of components within an image. Combined with vulnerability scanners like Grype, this enables organizations to enforce baseline security requirements—such as no critical vulnerabilities or specific library versions—before deployment.

### 4. Pod Security Standards
The policy enforces Pod Security Standards by blocking privileged containers, hostNetwork access, and hostPath volumes. These controls prevent container escape scenarios and limit the blast radius of potential compromises.

## Evaluation Criteria

Strong candidates will demonstrate:
- Understanding of OPA Rego syntax and Gatekeeper constraint templates
- Knowledge of Sigstore's keyless signing and verification workflows
- Familiarity with SBOM generation and vulnerability scanning tools
- Ability to design policies that are both restrictive and operationally practical
- Consideration for multi-cloud and on-premises consistency

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Assesses practical gating of dangerous Kubernetes patterns and practical CI design.

## Key Concepts

- Kubernetes manifest hygiene
- CI gates and lightweight scanners
- Pattern-based checks vs. full YAML parsing

## Code Example

```yaml
# failing manifest example
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx
  hostNetwork: true
```

```yaml
# passing manifest example
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:stable
```

```bash
# local verification
grep -R -E 'hostNetwork: true|hostPID: true|hostPath:' manifests || true
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you extend this to cover hostPort or readOnlyRootFilesystem checks?
- What are the advantages and trade-offs of simple grep checks vs YAML parsing?
